en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Thirty Birth Stories, Chapter on Kiṁchanda.
2. The Kumbha Jātaka “Who has appeared from the triple heaven into the sky,
illuminating the firmament like the moon?”
From his flanks rays of light stream forth,
like a flash of lightning in the sky;
he has cut through the windless, dense darkness in the air.
"You travel through the air and you stand [there];
has psychic power been well-cultivated by you,
even surpassing those deities who have not yet reached their goal?"
"Having come from the sky, you stand here saying, 'Buy a jar! Who are you, or whose jar is this?"
"Explain this matter to me, O brahmin.
"There is no jar of ghee, nor a jar of oil,
nor a jar of molasses, nor a jar of honey."
Listen to the many faults of Kumbha, the numerous defects residing within him;
having drunk from his throat, he fell headlong into a precipice.
A puddle, a cave, a sandalwood box, or a cesspool—
one might consume even much that is unfit for food;
therefore, buy this full jar!
Having drunk this and finding delight in his mind,
he wanders about like a bull seeking fodder;
longing for nothing else, he approaches it, singing and dancing.
"Buy this full pitcher! Having drunk from it,
one may wander naked and unclothed through the villages and the alleys between them."
"Buy this full pitcher; its drinker,
having drunk it, will rise up and tremble, his mind utterly deluded and sleeping far beyond the proper time."
Waving his head and his arms,
he dances like a wooden puppet;
buy this full jar from him!
Those who, having drunk [of this], lie as if scorched by fire,
and are even devoured by jackals,
undergo bondage, execution, and the loss of their wealth.
Buy this full pitcher! Having drunk from it,
one may speak what should not be spoken while sitting in an assembly,
having lost all sense of propriety.
Well-washed, free from stains, and fragrant— buy this full jar of hers!
Having drunk of which, one becomes haughty with turbid eyes.
"I think the whole earth belongs to me alone;
even a king of the four quarters is not my equal—
buy this full pitcher from me!"
Pride, arrogance, quarrels, and slander;
ugliness, nakedness, and flight—
this is the resort and abode of thieves and rogues.
"Buy this full pitcher of hers!
May there be families prosperous and flourishing,
with wealth numbering many thousands in this world!"
"Buy this full jar of hers,
which has cut off the deceit of inheritance;
[give] grain, wealth, silver, and gold."
Where they destroy the fields of cattle,
a destroyer of wealthy families—
buy this full pitcher from her!
Indeed, like a man whose appearance is distorted after drinking [liquor],
he reviles his mother and father;
he would even seize his own father-in-law and his daughter-in-law.
"Buy this full pitcher! Having drunk from it,
a woman of haughty appearance will revile both her father-in-law and her husband."
"Take even a slave or a servant; buy this full pitcher of hers!
For by drinking from it, a man might indeed kill."
If a recluse or a brahmin stands firm in the Dhamma,
one might even go to a state of misery because of that;
therefore, buy this full pitcher of merit!
Having drunk that by which they practice misconduct with body, speech, and mind,
they go to hell after having practiced such misconduct.
"Buy this full pitcher!
That which they could not obtain before even when begging and relinquishing much gold."
Having drunk that, he speaks falsely:
"Buy this full pitcher of hers!
For having drunk it, even when sent on an errand,"
When an urgent matter has arisen,
even when he is told, he does not understand the point:
"Buy this full jar of hers!"
Even those possessed of moral shame,
when intoxicated by passion, display a lack of shame;
even the wise and composed speak much when they are drunk.
Buy this full pitcher! Having drunk from it,
they lie down as a single heap,
fasting, on the bare ground in painful repose.
They bring forth ugliness and infirmity;
buy this full pitcher of hers!
For by drinking from it, men lie down with broken bodies.
Like cows struck by a club, they cannot withstand the force of Varuṇī;
it is like the speed of a well-trained man. Buy this full jar of hers!
That which people avoid as they would a fierce venomous snake—
being like poison in this world—
What man is worthy to drink it?
He whom the sons of Andhakaveṇḍu,
while sporting on the shore of the ocean, drank.
They attacked one another with clubs;
buy this full jar, for by drinking from it,
the ancient gods became intoxicated.
Having passed away from the eternal world of the Thirty-three gods,
such a person as that— knowing this present intoxicant to be useless,
O Great King— how could he drink it?
There is neither curd nor honey in this jar;
knowing this clearly, O King, do not buy it from me.
For in this way, these [goods] have been placed by me into this jar.
“O friend, you have told me everything exactly as it is.
“Neither my father nor even my mother is like you, such as you are.”
Desiring your welfare and compassionate,
and wishing for your supreme goal, I shall do your bidding today.
I give you five excellent villages.
A hundred female slaves, seven hundred oxen,
and these ten chariots yoked with thoroughbred horses—
you have become my teacher, desiring my welfare.
“O King, let there be the very best of female slaves for you;
let the villages and the cattle be yours alone;
and let the chariots yoked with thoroughbred horses be yours as well.”
"I am Sakka, the lord of the thirty-three gods.
Eat rice with meat and milk-rice with ghee,
and consume honey-cakes and sesame cakes."
"Thus, O Lord of Men, delighting in the Dhamma and beyond reproach,
may you go to the heavenly realm.
The Second Kumbha Jātaka.
